extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, assessment coordinators, curriculum committees, and educators responsible for undergraduate service courses and placement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and documented practices for departmental assessment of undergraduate mathematics (service and major) courses, including placement testing, course content alignment with client disciplines, outreach/liaison activities, and experimental integrated teaching models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate aims and methods to external colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty and administrative professional colleagues outside the department are much more willing and able to support your efforts if they know what you are trying to do and how you are trying to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicize plans and changes (departmental approval, university forums, student newspaper coverage). Establish liaisons to client units and create mechanisms (e.g., rotating seats) for advisors to participate so external stakeholders understand intent and process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriously respond to external recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inviting and receiving recommendations from others does not obligate you to accept them, only to seriously (and actually) respond to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat outside input as actionable: consider external expertise for data collection and analysis, document responses, and use positive precedents to build mutual trust despite initial departmental wariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continually repeat important messages and publicize
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as in a class, important messages have to be continually repeated, not just to the participants, but to interested observers as well. Publicity is not a dirty word, it is an important way of letting people know what you’re up to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple channels and repeated communications (forums, newsletters, press) so stakeholders and observers remain informed about assessment aims, processes, and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest real time and energy and plan for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective university relations require a great deal of time and energy. This means someone’s real time and someone’s real energy. If a department wishes to make this investment, it needs to carefully consider who will be involved and how their efforts will be assessed for the purposes of both salary and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designate accountable personnel, allocate workload, and ensure contributions to outreach/assessment count in evaluation, promotion, and compensation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active departmental support for student services
rubrics_metrics.description: Departmental faculty participate in training sessions, hold review briefings for tutors, lead study skills seminars, and sometimes allocate office hours directly to campus Academic Skills Centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with support units (peer tutoring, supplemental instruction), provide time and financial resources (often exceeding departmental budgets), and coordinate departmental involvement to support student success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal validation studies for placement testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct formal validation studies of existing placement tests to assess correlation with later course performance and to identify invalid items whose unit scores deviate from total test scores or fail to differentiate among students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tests are outdated (e.g., old MAA versions), perform item analysis and validation; consider adopting standardized measures (e.g., ACT) for some placements; revise mainstream placement instruments with advice from client faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align course content with downstream client needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey course topics used in advanced client-department courses, survey corresponding courses across the state, interview instructors, and have client faculty articulate their goals for the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use working groups to draft goal statements and new syllabi, perform question-by-question analyses of final exams, iterate revisions with client faculty, and be prepared to reduce topic coverage (example: 20% reduction) to match realistic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint faculty liaisons and sustain regular meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty liaisons from the department and client schools are appointed to oversee implementation; they meet regularly (e.g., monthly) to discuss changes and follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain ongoing liaison relationships rather than one-time consultations to ensure implementation, monitoring, and further course improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the assessment cycle: planning, implementing, responding
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment is a cyclic process with three main stages: (a) planning, (b) implementing, and (c) responding (Angelo & Cross).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stop at data collection; ensure findings lead to considered responses and actions. A voluntary approach can break the cycle if responsibility for response is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus assessment on faculty expectations and demonstrable student capabilities (avoid 'wish lists')
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask client instructors for a practical analysis of the mathematical knowledge required in their courses — not a 'wish list' but the skills they realistically expect students to bring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessments around specific, necessary capabilities articulated by instructors rather than broad or aspirational content statements; 'picking the instructor’s brain' helps identify what is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tests to assess only prior knowledge instructors expect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests should reflect only material that faculty articulate students will use during the semester — content the instructor does not plan to teach and assumes students already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use free-response problems constructed with instructors to target expected pre-course capabilities; avoid assessing material that will be taught in the course itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame assessments to encourage serious student participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform students that the test does not count toward their grade but will inform them about readiness, that the instructor cares about results, and that results may lead to course modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear framing increases effort and yields more useful data. Emphasize instructor interest and potential curricular consequences to motivate authentic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score items in diagnostic detail and provide rapid feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: On scantron sheets, each problem is graded on a five-point scale (from 'completely correct' to 'blank/irrelevant'); information is also coded about the steps students take toward a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record partial-credit-style diagnostics (e.g., whether a student 'differentiated correctly' or 'devised an appropriate representation'), return corrected papers with solutions and references within a week, and provide directed resources for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze results by problem-level success rates and patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute scores individually but focus on the proportion of the class that could do each problem; across courses look for patterns that inform departmental and institutional roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregated problem success rates to reveal common weaknesses (e.g., interpreting graphs, conceptual reasoning). Combine with students' course histories (non-identifiably) to interpret patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report findings strategically to maximize curricular influence
rubrics_metrics.description: While reporting to the entire faculty is appropriate, targeting findings at individuals and committees responsible for specific course levels/groups often yields greater curricular influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver tailored reports to those who can implement change (precalculus/calculus committees, course leaders) and include actionable recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assessment to resist lowering expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When many students lack necessary skills, departments sometimes 'water down' expectations; assessment should expose institutional consequences of such decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present evidence of downstream impacts to faculty and institutional committees to discourage ad hoc reductions in standards and to encourage systemic solutions (advising, prerequisites, course redesign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define multiple outcome criteria for integrated courses (TEAM example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess integrated-course initiatives on several dimensions: (1) student achievement, (2) student retention, (3) development of reasoning skills, (4) student attitudes, and (5) attitudes of other faculty toward required courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use validated instruments (e.g., TUCE pre/post) alongside professor-devised exams; compare performance on traditional vs. non-traditional items; measure retention and capture attitudinal data through surveys and anecdotal reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt active, cooperative learning and co-teaching models with technology where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrated TEAM course used two-hour blocks, mathematics and economics instructors co-teaching, pair/group problem solving, computers with software, instructors as facilitators, and group reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize lecturing, emphasize discovery and application to foster synthesis across disciplines, but recognize higher labor and resource costs (computer labs, co-teaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for practical constraints and faculty involvement in experimental courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Small institutions with computerized classrooms may find integrated, labor-intensive models worthwhile, but these delivery systems may be too expensive or impractical for widespread routine application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve more faculty from both departments early to reduce reluctance; accept that some topics may need curtailing; consider scalable adaptations (lab assignments, modules) for larger audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about small-sample generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Small enrollment experiments (e.g., TEAM with ~20 students per semester) may show positive results that might not replicate at larger scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat findings as promising but preliminary; plan pilot expansions and collect further data before broad adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assessment findings to influence institutional policy and curriculum design
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment results can inform campus-wide decisions (example: recommendation and adoption of a six-credit quantitative requirement) and aid in designing new courses to meet institutional goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link course-level assessment to institutional committees and policy makers; present evidence showing the need and design for curricular reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure assessment items to reflect client-discipline content balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems can be organized into content groups (e.g., non-calculus, differential calculus, integral calculus, differential equations) chosen to reflect the needs of different client disciplines (mathematics, physical sciences, engineering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design item sets whose topical balance mirrors client expectations (e.g., physical sciences emphasize differential calculus) to produce informative diagnostics for service-role evaluation.
